explanation: While joining a thread in a destructor guarantees thread completion and prevents termination, it introduces a potential performance anomaly. If the thread being joined takes a long or unpredictable amount of time to finish, the main thread (or whatever thread is performing the destruction) will block indefinitely waiting for the completion. Why It Fails: This turns the thread cleanup mechanism into a synchronization bottleneck, leading to difficult-to-debug latency spikes or freezes, especially if the object being destroyed is frequently created and destroyed.
code_example:
// ThreadRAII policy: join-on-destruction
~ThreadRAII() { if (t.joinable()) t.join(); } // Blocks the calling thread
practical_example: A web server handles requests by creating local `ThreadRAII` objects. If one request thread gets stuck in a long computation, the cleanup of that thread handle blocks the worker thread responsible for its destruction, potentially starving the thread pool.
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
